transcript:
[00:00] Derek Huang: Hey everyone, thanks for jumping on. Quick round of intros and then we'll dig into the POC scope.
[00:12] Lisa Moreno: Hi, Lisa here, Head of ML at BlueHarbor. We're reworking search rerank and want to see if Redwood can give predictable costs + latency.
[00:20] Tom Keegan: Tom, CTO. Main constraints: sub-200ms p95 for the consumer search UI and a monthly spend cap our CFO is pushing on.
[00:28] Derek Huang: Great. Maya from our SE team will cover batching/cache knobs and the benchmark recipe. Maya?
[00:33] Maya Ortiz: Hi all. Quick clarifying Qs: what's your average prompt length and distribution? Are these multi-turn sessions or single-query rerank?
[00:42] Lisa Moreno: It's single-turn — user search query plus 10 candidate documents, so our prompt is roughly 60-120 tokens typically. We sometimes attach product context which pushes to 140 tokens.
[00:52] Jamal Reed: And concurrency — peak is about 400 RPS for region us-west, but that's bursty; sustained is more like 80 RPS.
[01:01] Priya Singh: Also important — we need audit logs and SSO, and anything touching PII needs to stay in our VPC.
[01:08] Maya Ortiz: Noted. For unit economics, the two key knobs we'll tune are batching (how many requests per GPU micro-batch) and KV/prefix caching for repeated context. For rerank you get a lot of overlap in prefixes because candidate contexts share product text. That can drop tokens emitted per request when you cache KV.
[01:25] Tom Keegan: Can you give ballpark per-token numbers? Our finance model currently assumes $0.0008 per token which seems high.
[01:33] Derek Huang: Ballpark depends on model choice and quantization. For a 7B-ish dense open model on Redwood hosted, with basic batching and no caching, we typically see effective per-inference cost around $0.0002–$0.00035 per token at medium throughput. With prefix caching for shared contexts and aggressive batching, you can push down to ~ $0.00012–$0.00018 per token.
[01:54] Lisa Moreno: That's helpful — what's the tradeoff on latency when you batch? Our UI requires interactive latencies.
[02:00] Maya Ortiz: Right. Continuous batching improves throughput but can add headroom latency. We set a latency upper bound and then configure a micro-batch timeout (e.g., 5–10ms) and max batch size. For your p95 <120ms target and ~60–120 token inputs, we think a configuration with micro-batch timeout 6ms and batch sizes up to 16 balances both. We can also use per-request fast-paths on small inputs.
[02:22] Jamal Reed: How do we test this?
[02:24] Maya Ortiz: We'll run benchmarks on dedicated capacity (reserved GPU pool) to isolate variance. Test steps: 1) replay a 7-day trace at scale to reproduce tail latencies; 2) run controlled RPS sweeps with and without KV caching; 3) measure token throughput, p50/p95/p99 latencies, and cost-per-request; 4) sample outputs for quality checks.
[02:44] Tom Keegan: Timeline? CFO wants numbers within two weeks.
[02:48] Derek Huang: We can do an initial benchmark within 7 business days if we get the traces and top prompts today — Maya, is that realistic?
[02:55] Maya Ortiz: Yes. I can prepare a benchmark recipe and a small Jupyter notebook that computes per-token unit economics and token breakdown. We'll need a day to instrument and then schedule a 2-4 hour dedicated run window.
[03:07] Lisa Moreno: What about private deployment? We might need VPC or private for PCI-adjacent logs.
[03:11] Derek Huang: We offer Private deployment (VPC) — that adds setup time (2–3 weeks typical) and some differences in perf numbers since network topology differs. For the initial POC, we recommend hosted dedicated capacity in the region to get the unit-econ and perf baselines. If you need full private later, we can repeat the bench on that environment.
[03:28] Priya Singh: Audit logs and KMS — do you support customer-managed KMS and centralized audit export?
[03:33] Maya Ortiz: Yes, we support KMS integrations and streaming audit logs to your S3 or syslog endpoint. We'll include those docs after the call.
[03:40] Tom Keegan: Back to costs: can you model total monthly spend for our expected workload? I can give you RPS and average tokens.
[03:47] Derek Huang: Absolutely. If we assume 80 sustained RPS, avg 90 input tokens + 60 tokens generated (total 150 tokens per request), at $0.00018/token with caching assumptions that's about $0.027 per request. Multiply by 80 RPS * 3600 * 24 * 30 — that gets big. We'll send a spreadsheet with multiple scenarios (no cache, moderate cache, aggressive cache) and also show dedicated vs hosted price diffs.
[04:15] Jamal Reed: That per-request looks high vs our target; CFO target is <$0.02 per request.
[04:20] Maya Ortiz: Two levers to try: 1) increase cache hit rate by canonicalizing candidate contexts (most effective), 2) use a smaller model for initial rerank then fallback for hard cases. Combining both often halves effective per-request cost. We'll show example numbers in the model.
[04:36] Lisa Moreno: On model variants — do you support automatic fallback/rollouts? We want deterministic behavior for A/B tests.
[04:42] Derek Huang: Yes, Redwood supports rollout policies, canary deploys, and automatic fallback to a cheaper variant if SLOs are violated. We'll include recommended rollout configs for your A/B tests.
[04:52] Tom Keegan: For the benchmark, what metrics should we prioritize? CFO likes cost per MAU, but engineering wants p99.
[04:59] Maya Ortiz: Prioritize p95 latency and cost per 1k requests. Also capture p99 for risk, and model output quality (nDCG or pairwise accuracy on a labeled subset). We'll compute cost sensitivity to cache hit rate and batch size.
[05:14] Derek Huang: Ok, next steps recap: we provide a per-token cost workbook + bench recipe; BlueHarbor provides traces and top prompts; Redwood runs a dedicated-capacity benchmark next week and returns a results deck + recommended config.
[05:27] Lisa Moreno: That works. One last Q: any required on-prem hardware for dedicated bench?
[05:31] Maya Ortiz: No, we'll provision Redwood Dedicated GPUs in us-west. If you later want on-prem Private, that'll be a separate project.
[05:38] Tom Keegan: Thanks all. Let's keep the bench focused: 2-hour active sweep with trace replay, and then a 30-min quality review.
[05:46] Derek Huang: Great — we'll propose a 2–3 hour slot in the next Tue/Thu window. I'll send the spreadsheet today.
[05:53] Lisa Moreno: Thanks — talk soon.
[05:56] (call ended)
